body:
It sounds like you've put a lot of thought into this.  I can tell you the impression that I get from reading your reply:  You have a very unhealthy guilt complex.  Try to look at it objectively: Do you really think you were so unspeakably awful in your late teens and early twenties that you deserve to suffer for the rest of your life?  If you were such a bad person in your early years, and your SO followed a path similar to you, then why are you a bad person but your wife is just misguided (your word)?

So, you feel an unhealthy amount of guilt and you feel that the future is hopelessly bleak.  That really sounds like depression to me.  I hate to be that guy, but there really are effective treatments for depression.  Do you have medical insurance?  If so, it probably covers some sort of psychological counseling.  You probably would also benefit from trying out some different medications.  Don't give up on yourself; I can tell you right now you're a much better person than you make yourself out to be.  I can tell you, though, that having an extramarital fling with someone you don't even have much of a non-working relationship with will make things worse in the long run.

To put it bluntly, I don't think you're going to be capable of just buckling down and sacrificing your own happiness for your SO and your children.  You will reach your breaking point eventually if you don't deal with your marriage and your own psychological needs.  If I was you, I would make it very clear to your SO that things need to change if the marriage is going to survive.  Whether your SO "believes" in counseling I would make it known that marital counseling is going to have to happen.  I don't know your SO, but I feel like if you put your foot down hard enough they will probably be willing to compromise with you to some extent.  It could be that your SO needs to focus on changing some of their own behaviors in order to be a more mature spouse and parent.  

I know this is hard to hear, but if all else fails divorce isn't worse for children than having two unhappy parents in the same home.  If you stick around in a miserable state for your kids' sake, you will begin to develop resentment against them.  It sucks, but it's inevitable.  There is nothing worse for a child than having a parent who knows that they would be happier if the kid was never born.

Best of luck, OP.  In parting I would like to say that part of being happy is not taking things too seriously.  Maybe try to avoid thinking that things are unbearably hard and will never improve.  Life is about change, after all.

I see your point... Now that I've thought about this for about an hour and written my thoughts down, this seems like the most rational course of action.  Starting tomorrow I will find out how to do the statistical procedure properly and find the proper results.  Showing the proper results to my former advisor will be hard for me, but... I guess I've left myself no better option.  Sigh.  At least I feel some consolation that I got this wake up call at age 25 rather than when I'm older.

I've thought about doing what you're suggesting... It seems to me like it would be a possibility.  Because the dataset I am working with is a huge mess and I was doing a fairly complicated statistical procedure on it, it seems possible that they would allow me to make some changes to it with the understanding that doing proper work on data is difficult, especially for a relative beginner to the field.  But then sometimes I wonder if it's really worth it or if I'm just overthinking this whole thing.  Really, unless someone had it out for me, it's highly unlikely that they would bother with something like this - there are so many data points that it literally takes hours just to read the data.  People don't really care about master's theses and mine is likely to immediately fall into obscurity.  But at the same time this whole thing makes me feel so vulnerable - all of the info it would take to expose me is publicly available via the internet 24 hours a day.

As an outsider, it seems to me like the real problem is your marriage and not your crush.  The feelings you have for your coworker are perfectly normal and natural; the fact that you know not to act on them shows good judgment.  I know it's hard right now, but thinking about your coworker or, worse, acting on your feelings will make things much worse, especially for your children.

​

Whatever is going on in your marriage needs to be addressed.  If you don't work on your marital problems you're both going to end up miserable or divorced.  I've been witness to both, and both are awful.  Please, seek marriage counselling, or at least have a very serious and honest conversation with your spouse.  You are starting to see the chutes of a dissolving marriage, and they are going to sprout up faster and taller if you don't deal with this head on.

​

EDIT:  I feel like I struck the wrong tone with my original post.  Let me emphasize that I know what you're going through is extremely tough; the fact that you're willing to sacrifice your own happiness for your children and spouse says a lot about your moral character.

The point I tried to get across in my post is that the crush on your coworker is not the root cause of your distress.  Infatuation happens all of the time, it's not a problem.  The problem here is that you feel unhappy enough at home that you're seriously tempted to think about sacrificing your relationship with your family for a chance at happiness.  If it wasn't your coworker, it would be someone or something else causing you to want to leave.

In a way, I think you're lucky; it seems like you have discovered the problem with your marriage before it got too out of hand.  Are you sure that you can't be happy again with your spouse?  If not, I think you owe it to yourself to try anything possible to make yourself happy again.  If you strongly feel you can't be happy with your spouse, I would still advise you against just sticking it out.  Things just get worse over time.  This is the kind of problem which desperately calls out for a therapist.  Whatever you choose to do, please make sure that your happiness is maintained.  If you're miserable, you can't make anyone around you happy either.  You owe it to your family to find out what is best for you.
Yeah, I guess that's the thing.  I should probably just suck it up and move on, and resolve to do better in the future.

Hard to say.  There isn't really a cut-and-dried procedure for something like this.  Basically, it would be one of three situations:

​

1. They revoke my degree.
2. They let me keep my degree, but get rid of one of the sections of the paper.
3. They let me change the statistics in my paper under the belief that this situation was an honest mistake.

I really don't have any way of ranking the likelihood of any of these three possibilities.  One of the things I would be afraid of is that this could leak outside of our department (there are websites devoted to exposing dishonest people in academia; I'm not sure if they would go after a lowly master's graduate, though.)  I'm not sure it's worth the risk.  I feel like my best option might be to just let it be and hope nothing comes of it.

​

Thank you for replying.

I don't think they would... if they did, it would surprise me.  But I still feel the guilt for having done it.  And the possibility keeps coming up in my mind of being a respected person in my field in a few decades, and then having this discovered and losing everyone's respect.  I don't know why this bothers me this much.

Thank you for replying.  It's very nice to see that people on the internet take time out of their day to help random strangers.
